extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners, counsel, and parties in USPTO OED disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on filing and deciding Requests for Reconsideration under 37 C.F.R. §11.56(c) and on seeking suspension/waiver under 37 C.F.R. §11.3 in USPTO disciplinary proceedings. Covers timing, scope, evidentiary/diligence standards, permitted responses, and the high bar for waivers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-request and timing requirement for reconsideration (§11.56(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulation permits either party to make 'a single request for reconsideration or modification of the decision by the USPTO Director if filed within 20 days from the date of entry of the decision.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only one request is permitted and it must be filed within 20 days of the decision's entry. (In the case record, when an Initial Decision was redistributed, the respondent was allotted 14 days after service of the redistributed Initial Decision to appeal.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited scope of review for Requests for Reconsideration
rubrics_metrics.description: No request for reconsideration or modification shall be granted unless the request is based on newly discovered evidence or clear error of law or fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reconsideration is narrowly confined to (a) newly discovered evidence or (b) clear legal or factual error; it is not a vehicle for general disagreement, rehashing arguments, or raising 'new issues and inaccuracies' that do not meet those standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newly discovered evidence must be truly newly discoverable only with due diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: The requestor must demonstrate that any newly discovered evidence could not have been discovered any earlier by due diligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A showing that evidence is 'new' is insufficient unless the movant explains why it could not have been discovered sooner through reasonable diligence. Failure to establish this due-diligence barrier defeats reconsideration based on new evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Response timeframe to a Request for Reconsideration
rubrics_metrics.description: After such a request is filed, '[t]he other party may file a response to the request for reconsideration within 14 days of the filing of the request.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule contemplates a single response period of 14 days for the opposing party; the regulation does not provide for additional rounds (e.g., reply briefs) absent waiver.

rubrics_metrics.name: No allowance for Reply briefs under §11.56(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no allowance in the rule for a Reply brief, or any other filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the regulation does not permit replies, a party seeking to file a reply must obtain a suspension/waiver of the regulation under §11.3; absent such waiver, leave to file a reply should be denied. Simply asserting need to address 'new issues and inaccuracies' is not a basis for a reply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiver/suspension standard under §11.3 — 'extraordinary situation, when justice requires'
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursuant to 37 C.F.R. §11.3, '[i]n an extraordinary situation, when justice requires' any requirement of USPTO's regulations governing disciplinary proceedings that is not a statutory requirement may be suspended or waived by the USPTO Director sua sponte or on petition by any party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Waiver applies only to non-statutory regulatory requirements, must be grounded in an 'extraordinary' situation, and the Director may act sua sponte or on petition. The movant must show that justice requires suspension/waiver under this high standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiver is strongly disfavored and denied for preventable circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Waiver is strongly disfavored and will not be granted for circumstances that 'could have been prevented by the exercise of ordinary care or diligence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office cautions that the mere existence of a waiver provision should not be read as implying liberal waiver. Courts and the Office require that the circumstance be truly extraordinary and not something avoidable by ordinary care (citation: Nitto Chemical Indus. Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Office example of an 'extraordinary situation' (illustrative)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office's example of an extraordinary situation is when 'a flood or fire' prevented an applicant from timely submitting information for an application to practice before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This illustrative example signals that natural disasters or similarly unavoidable calamities are the type of events that may justify waiver; routine litigation disputes, missed procedural strategy, or disputes over 'inaccuracies' are not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motions seeking waiver or leave must identify authority and satisfy §11.3 standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A Motion for Leave that fails to identify any authority for the requested relief and does not demonstrate satisfaction of §11.3's 'extraordinary situation' standard is deficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motions should cite the governing regulation (e.g., §11.3) and present factual and legal support showing why justice requires waiver/suspension — conclusory statements (e.g., 'for addressing new issues and inaccuracies') are inadequate and justify denial.
